memories.memory_text: I was going over a play in my head when the plane jolted hard—next thing I knew, I was on my feet, leaning into the cockpit to check on the pilots.

I grabbed the rack above Dale when the plane jolted, then sat beside her and offered my candy bar—she shot me a look like I was some creep, but I told her I wasn't a stranger, not with my face on People magazine.
She asked if we were going backward, then gasped and pointed at the clouds—her voice was tight with fear, and I could feel the plane lurching, something wasn't right.
The sky turned red and the clouds started moving impossibly fast around the plane — I could feel Dale squeezing my hand like she was afraid she'd vanish.
I remember the cockpit door exploding open, wind tearing through the cabin, papers flying everywhere—I was on my feet in an instant, unbuckling and moving forward fast.
I lunged into the cockpit and grabbed the bucking yoke, fighting to pull the plane out of the dive as wind tore through the shattered windows.
Dale shouted some dumb joke about a man falling ninety stories while we were both yanking the controls, and for a second it cut through the panic—I actually wanted to hear how it ended.
I shouted to brace ourselves—I was locking onto that field up ahead as the only shot we had to land this thing.

I remember Dale suddenly stopping, staring at Zarkov like she’d seen a ghost, and then trying to back out fast—something about a magazine, NASA, and almost saying he was insane. I didn’t get it at first, but her look told me everything.

One second we were talking, the next—Zarkov pulls a gun and shoves it into Dale’s back, yelling about Earth being attacked. Red laser bolts are exploding the greenhouse around us, glass raining down, fire everywhere, and he’s jabbing me with the revolver, screaming 'Up the stairs—RUN!'
I saw Zarkov shove Dale into that mirror-bright capsule and I didn't think—I just leapt after her, the world exploding around us.
I jumped Zarkov, punched him in the gut, and tried to stop him from launching, but he slammed me back and hit a switch that made the capsule start whirling.
The spinning got worse, I grabbed Dale and held her close as the force slammed us against the wall—our bodies pressed together, barely able to move.
I remember holding Dale as we crashed through the fire, the capsule spinning, then slowing—my arms were locked around her, and when I saw Mongo’s molten surface rushing up, I thought we were dead.
I stepped forward, smiled, and said 'Hi!'—reaching out my hand like it was a normal first meeting, but the next thing I knew, a manacle snapped onto my wrist and I was slammed to the ground.

I grabbed Zarkov and shouted in his face—'You got us into this—HOW DO WE GET OUT?'—because we were being dragged through some twisted hall by armored goons and he was still yammering about Black Holes like it was a damn science fair.

I don’t know what Ming said next, but the way those armored men tightened their grip and the air went cold—I knew they were about to execute us. I locked eyes with him, ready to fight even if it was the last thing I did.
I was on the floor, completely overwhelmed—dozens of Amazons on top of me, pressing me down, and I could see Dale being dragged up the stairs, helpless.
I heard her scream my name—'Flash!!'—and something inside me snapped; I just exploded upward and broke free, charging after her.
I was so close to Dale—our fingertips just brushed—and then the step beneath me vanished, and I was falling, screaming into the dark.
I was falling through this dark, endless shaft, and all I could hear was Aura yelling to take a breath and grab her ankle when we hit the water—then suddenly, a massive splash swallowed everything.

I saw it through the glass—the lake of seething magma, glowing like hell itself, spinning slow and hot, feeding that weapon aimed at Earth. Aura said it was the plasma core, unstoppable, but I knew we had to try.

The Lizard Men—chained, shoveling gravel into the magma, guards shocking them when they fall. If they couldn't get up, those hooded men just threw them in. I saw one collapse… and vanish into the fire.

I grabbed Aura’s shoulders and demanded to know where Dale was—then she pulled me into a niche as soldiers passed, her body pressed against mine, and whispered that Ming intends to marry Dale. I could barely process it—Ming marrying Dale? It hit me like a shock I couldn’t shake.

I looked through the glass doors and saw rocket ships inside—real ones—and when Aura said I’d fly them, I snapped, 'I can’t fly a damn rocket ship!' Her teasing reply barely registered; all I could think was this mission just got a thousand times riskier.
I asked Aura why the moon kingdoms don’t team up against Ming, and then it hit me—what if they could? That moment, I saw it: not just fighting, but uniting as a real strategy.
I slammed my hand on the controls, sent the ship into a dive—Aura screamed, dropped the telepathic hood. I grabbed her wrists before she could stop me. I had to force her to let me reach Dale.
I had to hold Aura's wrists tight—she was fighting me, but I couldn't let go until she connected me to Dale. The planet was rushing up at us, but I didn't care—I wasn't losing her again.
I told Dale to fake them out and get to Zarkov—she was scared, chained up and about to be handed over to Ming, but she had to move fast and stay sharp.

When she said she was naked in a bathtub, I couldn't breathe—my voice broke, and for a second all I wanted was to touch her; then I just held on to the thought that she understood me, even without words.
I stared into Aura's eyes and almost sent Dale a final message, but then I realized it was pointless—sending words through her would be like handing a lettuce-leaf to a rabbit.
I jammed my hand into one of the serpent stump's holes, left it just long enough to make everyone think the worst, then yanked it out and threw the challenge back at Barin—'Your turn, Prince Barin.'

I called out to Dale mid-flight, telling her we were gonna do it first thing when we landed—she smiled and said I’d make her blush, like we had time for shyness with everything falling apart around us.

One second she was there, then a shadow fell over her—next thing I saw was that glow pulling her and her Hawkman up into a ship; I screamed 'I'm coming, Dale!' and told my Hawkman to climb, but he dove instead.
I climbed out of the capsule and heard Barin shout that I was casting a shadow—completely invisible, but my shadow was still there on the ground.
I snatched the ring from Ming’s hand and slammed it onto Dale’s finger—her gasp cut through the silence, and for a heartbeat, I knew she felt me there.
I drew the sword from the crystal block and held it before me. When it appeared like fire, Ming reacted sharply and said only his heir could pull it.

memories.memory_text: I'm up on the platform inside the glass tower, moving quickly—there's no time to waste. The mirror-bright object is pulsing, and the red sun outside makes everything feel like it's burning.
I remember slamming the TV off and shouting at that fool newscaster—this wasn't some random cosmic accident, it was an attack, planned by a mind. I could feel the truth of it burning in my chest.
I pulled the revolver on Munson when he hesitated—calmly, firmly. I had to make him understand: we were launching now, or Earth was finished.
I saw the red bolts striking the greenhouse, glass exploding—I shouted into the chaos, demanding Munson show himself or I’d shoot.
I had the revolver aimed at Munson's back—he was just walking away, leaving us all to die—I shouted that I couldn't take it off alone, that if he wouldn't come, who else would I find?

I saw the recognition flash in Dale's eyes when she remembered me from that PEOPLE magazine article — the one that called me insane after I left NASA. I hesitated, then confirmed who I was, watching her try to backtrack her words.

I pointed the gun at Flash and told them to go up the stairs ahead of me. The greenhouse was breaking apart from laser strikes and fire, and I urged them to move quickly. Earth was under attack — we had no time to waste.
I tore the foliage aside and revealed the capsule—bright as a mirror, untouched by the storm—then yanked the door open and told them I’d shoot if they didn’t get in.
Dale was backing away, refusing, and Flash was about to jump—so I shoved her hard, off-balance, into the capsule before he could act.
I forced Flash to the seat and shouted at him to put his foot on the red pedal—then he attacked me, but I twisted away and hit the switch just as I was falling.
The G-force crushed me against the wall, my face straining, barely able to speak—each word took everything: friendship, the world ending, and the three of us having to stop it.
I watched my capsule climb into the sky, spinning fast and untouched by their laser fire—each bolt glancing off like sparks against steel.
I saw Mongo's molten surface rushing toward us, a sea of amber fire, and I crawled to the controls—my hands shaking as I flipped switches, but nothing responded.
By God, we did it! We made it!
I don't know where we are.
I told Flash to extend his hand—it’s the universal gesture of friendship—and seconds later, they slammed a manacle on his wrist and threw him down; they were capturing us, not greeting us.
I shouted 'You inhuman fiend!' after seeing that armored man throw himself onto his sword—Ming ordered it like it was nothing, just to prove a point.
I remember thinking how perfectly this leads us to Ming—getting to him is our only chance to save Earth, even if Flash just wants to escape.
Flash is looking for me. He said he has to find Dale and 'that nut Zarkov' and try to save Earth.
I was shackled and dragged by soldiers along the catwalk, forced to witness the seething lake of plasma that flared blindingly with each shovelful of gravel dumped into it.
I called him a devil—Ming—standing there in that hellish light, forcing plasma toward annihilation, and I begged him to use his science for peace instead, to be remembered as blessed, not cursed.

I saw Earth burning inside that cube—fire sweeping over everything, even the clouds, and then it was gone, reborn with strange new continents. It wasn't just destruction; it was a twisted rebirth, and he called it pleasant.
I lunged at the crystal block and grabbed the hilt, pulling with all my strength—but the sword wouldn't move. No matter how hard I strained, it was as if it were fused to the stone.
I woke to a hand on my shoulder and saw a serving girl leaning over me—then realized it was Dale in disguise, her eyes fierce with urgency beneath that cloak.
My hands vanished—completely invisible—but I could still feel them. I picked up a pebble and tossed it between my unseen hands to show Dale it wasn't gone, just hidden.
I watched my hands slowly reappear, fading back into view as if painted over by invisible ink. I wondered—could we control this effect? But then the hawkmen came.

I saw Flash clinging to the edge, straining to pull Barin up, and when Vultan demanded he let him fall, I spoke — 'Call it what you want, Vultan — compassion — mercy: let us teach you the meaning of these words.'
I looked Vultan in the eye and asked him, 'What'll you have -- death or dishonor?' and when he hesitated, I knew the choice was his to make.
I told Flash to sit and wait for my signal—when I say zero, he punches the button. No room for error.
I shouted 'Eureka! I did it!' the moment I saw the blinding blue light fade and felt the helmet turn on its own — Flash was gone, completely invisible, just as the calculations predicted.

Right after Flash stepped out and his shadow hit the ground, a terrible whining hum tore through the sky — the earth shook, brown foliage rained down, and Barin screamed at me, 'Zarkov! What have you done?'

I heard the thud of a body falling, then silence—until the scrape of a key in the lock broke it, and the door swung open on its own. Then Flash's voice: 'It's me!'—and in that moment, I knew we weren't doomed after all.
I watched the needle edge closer to red, and I knew—no calculations left, no way out. I said the words aloud: we've lost, unless a miracle happens.
